title: Modern Policy Optimisation and RL for Language Models
oneLiner: The practical toolkit of today's RL (parallel actors, smarter advantage estimates and PPO), and how the same ideas teach chatbots to give answers people prefer.

what.html:
Modern policy optimisation runs many copies of the environment at once, estimates "how much better than expected" each action was with GAE, and updates with PPO, which caps how much any action's probability can change per update. For language models, each word (token) is an action and a whole reply is an episode. RLHF learns a reward from human comparisons and optimises it with PPO; DPO skips the reward model and learns straight from the comparisons; GRPO compares several sampled answers to each other.

Everyday versionA writing coach doesn't give marks out of 100; they say "this version is better than that one". RLHF and DPO learn from exactly that kind of feedback.

why.html:
• PPO + GAE is the default algorithm in much of deep RL.
  • These methods are how large language models are aligned with what people want.
  • Knowing the moving parts (reward model, reference model, KL penalty) explains many of their quirks.

how.title: Many workers at once
how.html: Run lots of environments in parallel so training data aren't all from one moment. A3C lets workers update shared weights whenever they're ready; A2C waits and makes one big batch.

how.title: Better 'how good was it?' estimates
how.html: GAE adds up the critic's surprises over the next few steps, each weighted a bit less: 1.0 + 0.8 × (−0.2) + 0.64 × 0.5 = 1.16. One knob (λ) trades noise against bias.

how.title: PPO on a batch
how.html: For each sample: ratio × advantage, but never give credit for moving the ratio beyond 1 ± ε. Four samples give 2.40, −0.80, 1.20 and −1.60, averaging 0.30.

how.title: A chatbot is a policy
how.html: State = prompt plus words so far; action = next token; episode = the whole reply; reward = how good the reply is, usually given only at the end.

how.title: Learning a reward from comparisons
how.html: People pick the better of two replies. A reward model learns scores so that the preferred reply's score is higher. PPO then improves the chatbot against those scores, with a penalty for drifting too far from the original model.

how.title: Skip the reward model: DPO
how.html: DPO directly raises the preferred reply's probability and lowers the rejected one's, relative to the original model. A margin of 0.7 gives a loss of 0.403; sharpening to 1.3 lowers it to 0.241.

how.title: Compare answers in a group: GRPO
how.html: Sample several answers to the same question, score them (e.g. correct or not), and reinforce those above the group average. No critic network needed.

demo.html: A toy model with four possible answers learns from 400 pairwise preferences using DPO. Watch the best answer gain probability while the policy stays near the original; change β to see how tightly it's held.

example.html:
Why PPO takes the min after multiplying. A sample with ratio 0.7 and advantage −1: the unclipped term is −0.70, the clipped term 0.8 × (−1) = −0.80. PPO takes the smaller (more pessimistic), −0.80. If you took the smaller ratio first (0.7) and then multiplied, you'd get −0.70 and lose the safety property.

Supplementary PPO's ratio uses the policy that generated this batch; the RLHF penalty uses the frozen original model. They are different models with different jobs.

misunderstandings: PPO forces all ratios into [1 − ε, 1 + ε].
It removes the incentive to move further; ratios can still leave the range.
The reference model is PPO's old policy.
Old policy = batch reuse; reference = long-term anchor.
It learns from preference pairs directly.

A language model is a token-level policy with end-of-response rewards. RLHF trains a Bradley–Terry reward model on human comparisons and optimises it with PPO using the shaped reward r_φ − β log(πθ/π_ref); the reference anchor is distinct from PPO's old policy. DPO optimises −log σ(β·margin) on preference pairs directly (0.403 → 0.241). GRPO uses group-normalised scores of sampled answers without a critic; IPO, ORPO and SimPO vary DPO's assumptions.
